newsitem.title: CANADA: Gulf Canada CEO expects no rival bid for Clyde.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Canada CEO expects no rival bid for Clyde.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources Ltd. Chief Executive J.P. Bryan said on Friday he considered the odds of a rival bid surfacing for Britain's Clyde Petroleum Plc to be slim.
British analysts have said a competing offer of at least 120 pence per share would have to be launched to pull Clyde from Gulf's grasp.

Calgary, Alberta-based Gulf on Wednesday said it planned to offer Clyde shareholders 105 pence per share cash in a debt-funded hostile takeover bid valued at 432 million British pounds ($720 million).
Clyde quickly urged its shareholders to reject the offer.
"I don't think anybody's going to pay 120 (pence) unless its based on some information we didn't know about," Bryan said Friday in an interview in Calgary.
Industry sources said numerous investment bankers have assembled large files of financial data on Clyde for prospective purchasers over the past several months.

Recently, the most aggressive oil industry acquisitors have been U.S.-based companies, which would face a challenge wringing value from a rival Clyde bid because of the strength of the British pound against the U.S. dollar, he said.

Bryan, who was in London earlier this week to make the takeover announcement, said he had yet to meet with the major investors of Clyde, which include six financial institutions, to sell them on Gulf's offer.
He did, however, have a short conversation with Clyde Chairman Malcolm Gourlay who "curtly" told Bryan that Gulf offer was inadequate, he said.
Gulf's own shareholders on Friday continued to react positively to the Clyde deal and earlier news of a major natural gas discovery in Indonesia.
Gulf shares in Toronto closed up C40 cents to C$10.30 ($7.52), a new 52-week high.
The company, which already has debt of over C$1 billion, said it arranged financing with the Bank of Montreal to fund the deal.

If it was successful in acquiring Clyde, Gulf would pay down the debt with a series of Canadian oil and gas asset sales, an initial public offering of 20 percent of its Indonesia subsidiary and a C$100 million equity issue.

Bryan confirmed that Gulf had considered a bid for Clyde as early as the spring of 1995, but the company had yet to gain credibility from the investment community after he took control of the large producer, which was then struggling.
Since then, acquisitions have also made Clyde more attractive, he said.
The British firm's assets include oil and gas producing properties in the North Sea, Australia and Indonesia.
